responseSet.title: Interpretation and Working through in Psychotherapy of Children: A Case Study,
responseSet.authorMast: Maurice J. Rosenthal and  Sritham Thanaphum
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Interpretation and Working through in Psychotherapy of Children: A Case Study1,212

Maurice Rosenthal MD and Sritham Thanaphum MD

Sritham Thanaphum

Sritham Thanaphum  

Introduction

Lack of introspectiveness in children makes the “working through” process in their psychotherapy difficult to follow. Using three sessions from the therapy of a latency aged boy as a paradigm, the highlights of “working through” could be demonstrated. Following an interpretation that the boy acted out for counterphobic reasons, subtle inferences from the boy's subsequent behaviour made it possible to deduce that the interpretation had made a significant impact. One inference was that the boy symbolically emulated the act of the interpretation itself. The struggle in assimilating the contents of the interpretation followed. The “working through” seemed regulated by a “safety principle” (Sandler, 1960). Insight was evident in acknowldgment of a real inferiority.

The following paper is offered as a contribution to the understanding of the therapeutic process in interpretative psychotherapy with children. A microscopic examination of the clinical data of three sessions of therapy will be undertaken for this purpose.

The type of therapy that was employed belongs probably to the type of analytically oriented play therapy of school-aged children, which has been the main form of therapeutic intervention at American child guidance clinics for over twenty-five years (Witmer, 1947).

There has been a paucity of literature on children's cases pertaining to the middle range effects of individual interpretations; in other words, to the detailed study of segments of “working through” longer than a portion of one interview, but shorter than many interviews. This range is ideal for studying the latent and disguised effects of given interpretations. The present paper is a study in this relatively neglected area.

The delayed and hidden influence of an interpretation is a major problem in the psychotherapy of children, much more so than is the case in therapy with adults. It undermines the confidence of the therapist in his understanding of the child, and consequently in his faith in the utility of the therapy itself.

responseSet.title: D. E. M. Gardner: Susan Isaacs: A First Biography. Methuen Educational Ltd., 1972. Price £1.50.
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

D. E. M. Gardner: Susan Isaacs: A First Biography. Methuen Educational Ltd., 1972. Price £1.50.

Frances Tustin

Frances Tustin

Frances Tustin  

Reading this book was both a sad and joyful experience. On the one hand, it brought home sharply that human life is short. On the other hand, it was uplifting as evidence that psychological realities survive the body's decay.

The writer, Miss Dorthy Gardner, and Dr. D. W. Winnicott who wrote the Foreword, died quite recently: Susan and Nathan Isaacs some years ago. But their ideas live on and the extent of their influence on the course of human development cannot be measured. To have this loving and well-documented record of the life of Susan Isaacs is an inspiration both to those of us who had the privilege of knowing her and to those of a younger generation who are the heirs of what she struggled to conceptualise and to put into practice. As Miss Gardner says in her Preface, “Whether or not she is remembered, her influence will live; but to forget the woman would be a loss to those who find inspiration in seeing great values expressed in a human life”. Dr. Winnicott catches the spirit of the book when he writes: “This attempt at a reconstruction will serve its purpose if it brings Susan alive to those who never knew her, so that some may feel inclined to read her books by being introduced to her as a struggling, striving and radiant human being”.

This introduction to the struggles which lay behind the calm Susan Isaacs whom I knew was a revelation. We learn of her joys and sorrows in a none-too-easy family home in the stark and sombre Lancastrian village in which she was born. We read of her struggles to enter university in spite of financial difficulties and of having left school at fifteen. (She learned the Greek and German necessary for university entrance in three months!). We are not surprised that she graduated from Manchester University with a First Class Honours Degree in Philosophy and a Graduate Scholarship to Cambridge. However, she was turning from Philosophy to Psychology, and this finally led her to Psychoanalysis.

On being asked by Sir Percy Nunn to take charge of and to initiate the Child Development Course in London University we learn, through her letters, of the conflict between her intense interest in psycho-analytic work with individual patients, and her capacity to contribute to education both through her pioneer work in the Malting House School and her natural flair for understanding children. At first she felt she could not accept the Headship of the Child Development Department. That, in the end, she did do so has changed the lives of many students who entered that course with her and later with Dorothy Gardner.

responseSet.title: Therapeutic Pre-School Groups
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Therapeutic Pre-School Groups**

Lydia Mundy

Lydia Mundy

Lydia Mundy  

Introduction

Clinical intervention is usually not one of Primary Prevention as defined by Emanuel Miller a few years ago. However, an attempt of this kind is being made in England at Woolwich by Dr. David Morris, Paediatrician, and Mrs. Gordon, Psychotherapist, in one aspect of their work in which they link up with the Obstetrician. The next best undertaking is secondary prevention at an early stage; and a number of psychiatrists and psychotherapists have been, and are, seeing mothers with infants with disturbed behaviour individually. But the number of workers so involved seems comparatively small.

There are also very few reports in the literature about therapeutic group work at the toddler stage. The most relevant publications are to be found in the Psychoanalytic Study of the Child: “The Treatment of the Under-Five by way of his Mother”, Erna Furman, 1957; discussed by others at the American Association of Child Analysis, 1966, and taken up again by Augusta Alpert, 1967. Dr. Alpert discusses indications and contraindications for therapeutic intervention, in what she calls the “pre-nursery” via the mother. The physical set-up for this work at the Child Development Centre, New York, seems to be somewhat similar to ours, but the method, although regrettably not described in detail, seems to be somewhat different (as a large team seems involved there).

At the Wessex Unit (Southern England) we run small nursery groups for children aged 2-5 years, attending with their mothers. In our set-up this method of joint inter-active groups was first conceived by Dr. Christopher Haffner, Medical Director of the Unit, and first put into practice by him as early as 1958! (His own publication on the subject being overdue, but was quoted by Rogers, 1965.) Each group consists of three to four mothers, attending with their toddlers once- or twice-weekly for one and a half hours.

The physical facilities are a large tiled room (non-slip tiles) with floor heating and a small pool with bath-temperature water (therefore called the poolroom); a small water-trough on casters; a sunk sandpit; three large square wooden boxes, open on one side with a large round hole (window) on another, useful for “house-play” (going to “sleep” in it, etc.); otherwise a variety of the usual nursery toys.

responseSet.title: Dynamic Assessment of a Clever Boy with Learning Inhibitions
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Dynamic Assessment of a Clever Boy with Learning Inhibitions**

Patricia Radford

Patricia Radford

Patricia Radford  

Ekstein (1969) noted that for a child to be ready to learn formally at school he must have acquired basic trust, autonomy, the capacity to accept controls from outside, inner and outer discipline and socialised initiative. It will become clear from the diagnostic assessment that Terry had not reached such a state, but rather that there were truly pathological difficulties with regressions and fixations to or at the level where there was no learning readiness and where the solution of a task was made impossible because of the lack of a capacity for resolution of any conflict. In the environment of which he was a part his problems could not be recognised until he was thrust into the school situation. The complex phenomena of learning impotence within the school and social setting could then be seen as an expression of the total personality distortion, stultifying development and interfering seriously with all his relationships.

Terry was referred to the hospital at the age of eight years from two sources; from his general practitioner who was concerned about his somewhat bizarre behaviour, his isolation and lack of social relationships; from his school, where his inadequacy in the school situation had become even more apparent with his transfer to the junior department. Originally he had been seen when he was six years old by the paediatricians at the hospital for complaints of recurring sick headaches for which no physical cause was discovered. His mother had appreciated that the headaches were related to Terry's reluctance to attend school where he was considered to be educationally sub-normal. He could not read, write, nor had he any concept of number when he moved to the junior school. He was reported to be a difficult pupil, mostly withdrawn and likely to be violent if pressure were put on him to participate in class activities. However, his new headmistress was impressed by his considerable oral ability and she persuaded him to dictate his disturbingly unreal fantasies on to tape. The educational psychologist was asked to investigate; Terry's innate abilities were disclosed in the results of the psychological tests—the findings on the Weschler Intelligence Scale for Children were in the range of 130-145 I.Q. The parents were now prepared to seek help for the educational problems; they had seemingly been unconcerned about the severe personality disorder; it was much later in mother's treatment that we learnt how much she had had to deny it because of her fear that Terry was mad.

responseSet.title: Reflections on Problems Faced by Interdisciplinary Staffs in Residential Schools for Maladjusted Children
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Reflections on Problems Faced by Interdisciplinary Staffs in Residential Schools for Maladjusted Children

Thomas Lopez and Gladys Jones-Cuellar

Gladys Jones-Cuellar

Gladys Jones-Cuellar  

In this paper some thoughts concerning problems faced by professional staffs employed in (what seems to be) the typical residential school for the education of the maladjusted child in the London area, are presented. Two divergent tendencies are focused on: one, the tendency on the part of these professionals to acknowledge that the problems posed for them by these schools are essentially new problems—problems which have not yet been successfully resolved—and to attempt, actively, to come to grips with them; the other, the tendency on their part to retreat from this kind of acknowledgment and from the anxiety it arouses.

We owe our acquaintance with the schools to our being (collectively) employed in three of them as child psychotherapists, and to discussions we have had with colleagues employed in a number of others. Though for the sake of simplicity only the residential school is discussed, we believe the views presented here can, with appropriate modification, be readily extended to the non-residential school for the education of the maladjusted child (Jackson, 1970) as well. [For an excellent general survey of the subject, as well as a substantial bibliography, see Beedell (1970). In this journal, for articles dealing with the problems posed by treatment of children in residential settings, see Folkart (1964, 1967) and MacCarthy (1966).]

The Schools and the Children

The schools under discussion are multidisciplinary endeavours. Their staffs are made up by three disciplines: (1) the teaching staff, which includes the headmaster or headmistress, his or her deputy and the teachers; (2) the psychiatric team, which includes a psychiatrist and one or more educational psychologists, child psychotherapists and psychiatric social workers, and (3) the house-staff, which includes a domestic bursar and a number of house mothers and fathers. In each school, the headmaster or headmistress is the person principally in authority.

The children in residence, typically have backgrounds in which chronically inadequate home lives are prominent features; their parents being often people who are but marginally adaptive in a social sense. Diagnostically, they tend to be children whose personalities are deficiently developed, or impoverished, rather than children with the primary diagnosis of neurosis, psychosis or borderline condition.

responseSet.title: Over-Determination of a Fantasy Involving Compulsive Rituals and Thoughts
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Over-Determination of a Fantasy Involving Compulsive Rituals and Thoughts

Dora Lush

Dora Lush

Dora Lush  

In this paper, it will be shown how a fantasy described by the patient contained the roots of many of her unconscious emotions, many of which had not yet emerged in the treatment.

The terms “fantasy” and “phantasy” will be used here as suggested by Susan Isaacs (1952) when she differentiated the two terms, as follows: “The English translators of Freud adopted a special spelling of the word ‘phantasy’ with the ‘ph’ in order to differentiate the psycho-analytical significance of the term, i.e., predominantly or entirely unconscious phantasies, from the popular word ‘fantasy’, meaning conscious day-dreams, fictions and so on”. However, even a conscious fantasy has deeper significance and the fantasy described in this paper masked unconscious phantasies and was rich in latent content.

The Patient

Anne was twelve years old and in her first year at secondary school when she was referred to the Child Guidance Clinic. The presenting symptom was worry over homework, over which she spent several hours every evening, but, as well as this, Anne's life was dominated by anxiety, fears and phobias. She was obsessionally clean and tidy and very slow in washing and dressing. She was frightened of going anywhere alone and felt sick on buses. She was very anxious over what people would think of her and the slightest reprimand at school made her want to go to another school. She was paranoid towards her schoolfellows and constantly imagined them talking about her.

Anne was the eldest of several children in a prudish religious family who reinforced some of her obsessional characteristics. She was of low average intelligence and found the school work difficult, but this was not the cause of the hours spent on it. She would obsessionally copy again any work containing the slightest error or smudge. Even when teachers told her she would not be punished for untidy work, she continued at her self-punitive task, leaving herself no time for leisure pursuits.

History

Mother reported that pregnancy and birth had been normal. Anne was breast fed for six weeks and mother reported no feeding difficulties. Anne was clean and dry at two years old and even previous to that, she was always unhappy if she soiled or wet herself. She was fifteen months old when the next sibling, a girl, was born.

responseSet.title: Paul Nordoff and Clive Robbins: Therapy in Music for Handicapped Children, with a foreword by Benjamin Britten. Victor Gollancz, London, 1971. Price £1.80.
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Paul Nordoff and Clive Robbins: Therapy in Music for Handicapped Children, with a foreword by Benjamin Britten. Victor Gollancz, London, 1971. Price £1.80.

Geoffrey Elkan

Geoffrey Elkan

Geoffrey Elkan  

This book is an account by an American composer and an English music therapist of the evolution of a technique of music therapy with individual children and with groups of children. The authors have worked alongside educators, psychiatrists, neurologists, speech therapists and others—both in Europe and America—dealing with children suffering from severe functional and/or organic handicaps. The detailed case-material, including excellent photographs, conveys to the reader a vivid impression of the individuality of the children and of the authors’ relationship with them.

In their work with individual children, the authors have developed an “exploratory” (diagnostic) technique in which the senior author, seated at the piano, offers the child the use of drum, drumstick and cymbal to use as he wishes. What is of especial importance is that the authors are receptive and attentive to what the child brings, and only then try to give musical expression to this for the child through improvisation at the piano. This appears to be comparable to the analytic situation in which the therapist is receptive and attentive to the child's unconscious communications and attempts to put these into words for the child. The authors then go on to see how the child responds to new musical stimuli; they regard this as an indication of the child's capacity to relate to the therapist as an external object and also an indication of the range of emotions which the child is ready or willing to experience with him.

The authors describe some of the resistances to emotional involvement and the moments of breakthrough. An example is the case of a seven-year-old autistic girl (“Rosita”), where the sequence from withdrawal through to animation and delight at a shared experience as she joined the therapist in playing and singing is vividly illustrated in words and photographs.

With those children who are unable to use the instruments, or indeed to come beyond the doorway, the therapist improvises music expressing the mood of the child (as the therapist senses it) as a means of establishing contact. With autistic children especially, this phase of treatment in which “therapy had to start by setting any habitual mode of behaviour or any fragmentary response into a musical context” could last for many months before the child himself used an instrument.

responseSet.title: The Object Relations of a Borderline Psychotic Child and Their Connection with His Inability to Learn
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Object Relations of a Borderline Psychotic Child and Their Connection with His Inability to Learn

Rachel Newbolt

Rachel Newbolt

Rachel Newbolt  

Working for three years with Tim, a borderline child, gave me insight into his negative and often terrifying view of object relationships which throws light on the almost total inability to learn which is often seen in such children. I propose to show how he communicated his difficulties, at first in primitive materials only, without speech, and later in “dramatic” play and words.

Tim's failure to develop normally was first discovered in the routine medical examination prior to his admission to school at the age of five. It was impossible to test him because of his fearful and negative behaviour and he was referred to the Child Guidance Clinic and taken on for twice-weekly psychotherapy. In the early sessions he could not stay with me alone for long and each parent and his young adolescent sister spent part of a session with him in turn, giving me the opportunity to observe their handling of him.

Tim's mother had suffered a post puerperal depression after the birth of each of her children and was subsequently sterilised when he was three years old after the termination of her third pregnancy. It is possible that she made a physical attack on her son in the first few days of his life. He was looked after by his grandmother for several weeks and subsequently both parents played an equal part in his care. His mother tended to take a tense and defeatist view of Tim and to feel isolated with the problems, while remaining unable to accept fully all the social work help offered. Tim's father was an extremely rigid and unsophisticated man with a severe speech defect, who seemed quite bizarre until one got to know him. Both parents made some move in maturation over the years but remained basically very controlling with Tim which unfortunately meant that they could not happily accept his more spontaneous behaviour when he started, in the eyes of school and clinic, to improve.

The first time I saw Tim, he clung to his mother while she talked to the psychiatric social worker. I noted that he looked at me occasionally but looked away at once if I looked at him. On his second visit, he stayed with me for a few minutes, covering his eyes with one hand and trembling all over. I acknowledged his fear of me and my room which he shut out, then got his father to join us but he tried so anxiously to thrust the child into activity that I terminated this part of the session. When his mother came in, she was able to leave him alone while she talked to me and he put out a hand now and then to touch one of the toys and then quickly withdrew. His mother told me he had come willingly today for the first time. In his third week he was hiding and peeping out at me when I went to fetch him.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Marion Milner: On Not Being Able to Paint. Heinemann Educational Books Ltd., London, 1971. Price 90p

Dilys Daws

Dilys Daws

Dilys Daws  

In this illuminating book (now re-printed in paper-back form) Marion Milner's courageous enquiry into the limits of her creativity in painting becomes a creative analytic process in its own right, and it is fascinating to see how in each stage as logical thought and insight come together her painting reaches a stage further in liberation.

She describes how “original work in painting … would demand facing certain facts about oneself as a separate being” and she has the courage to begin facing these and the “dangers inherent in the nature of imagination”. She discovers that an emphasis on outline comes from the “emotional need to imprison objects rigidly within themselves” and a fear that “letting in imagination meant letting in madness”. As she learns to let go the outline her drawings take on more life and when she finds “a way of thinking about the connection between madness and sanity” she is able to think more freely about the meaning of her drawings. She discovers in her free drawings the violence of her rebellion against her inner authorities and says “I had not thought that such an inner fight might interfere with attempts at creative activity … I had not fully realised that the restraint of one's will imposed by authority could at times feel like a threat to one's whole existence, an attempt to separate one from the very source of one's creative relation to the world”.

Marion Milner is then able to deal positively with the idea of separateness and suggest “It seemed then that one could attempt to avoid the sorrow of change and separation and loss by spiritually enveloping what one loved and taking it inside oneself, but that this did not really solve the problem; for there was still the fear that by having it inside one might have destroyed it. To an established painter, who knows that he can successfully bring what he has taken inside himself back to life in the outside world as a painting, there may be less anxiety in this act of spiritual envelopment in order to paint”.

responseSet.title: Psychotherapy with a Boy from a Children's Home
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Psychotherapy with a Boy from a Children's Home

Mary Boston

Mary Boston

Mary Boston  

Introduction

In this paper I should like to describe some aspects of the treatment of a boy “in care” who has been deprived of family relationships and continuous mothering at least since his second year of life.

As is well known, such children, whose experiences of parent figures have been so unfortunate and unreliable, tend to be difficult to make contact with and to respond with suspicion and hostility when a new relationship is offered. Bowlby (1946) suggested that such experiences may lead to the development of a delinquent character unless treatment is undertaken at a very early age. Many writers have stressed the damage to emotional and intellectual development caused by early deprivations in the relationship with the mother (e.g., Burlingham, D. and Freud, A. (1944), Williams, Jessie M. (1961)). Williams (1961), pointed out that damage to personality growth may be sufficiently serious to prevent successful foster home placement. Residential care may have to be provided either because of continuing environmental deprivation or as an attempted solution for the difficulties which have already arisen. Winnicott (1956, 1965) suggests that in some cases placement may be necessary before psychotherapy or psycho-analysis can be considered. These children certainly present considerable problems in residential care (Tod, 1968) and the question of what kind of therapy is appropriate and possible becomes an urgent one. Once-weekly psychotherapy is often thought to be difficult, with a doubtful outcome (Yeo, 1960) and has sometimes been found to increase the problems in the home (Brill & Thomas, 1964). Dockar-Drysdale (1968) considers that certain “frozen” children who have never had the experience of loving someone else as a separate person are not ready for psycho-analytic work with interpretations in the transference but need first to be provided with “primary experience”.

My experience with the child to be discussed (who was possibly not “frozen” in Mrs. Dockar-Drysdale's sense) is that interpretative work along psycho-analytic lines is possible but that there are very considerable difficulties in coping with the violent feelings which are aroused. This is in line with Winnicott's experience that when the patient starts to make an object relationship, antisocial or destructive behaviour may be manifested to such a degree that treatment may either become impossible or be interfered with by outside agents. Nevertheless Winnicott says “in every case if psychotherapy is to be successful, the patient must be seen through one or many of these awkward phases of manifest antisocial behaviour” (Winnicott, 1963). I have found once-weekly treatment may be insufficient to enable the patient to work through his hostility to a stage when more trusting relationships can be experienced.

responseSet.title: A Study of a Residual Autistic Condition and its Effect upon Learning
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

A Study of a Residual Autistic Condition and its Effect upon Learning**

Shirley Hoxter

Shirley Hoxter

Shirley Hoxter  

Introduction

The main concern of this paper will be to study some factors which appear to have impeded or enhanced one particular boy's capacity for growth. Christopher, usually known as “Piffie”, commenced psychotherapy with me at the age of three and a quarter years. He attended four times weekly for the most part, until he was eight and a quarter when treatment was terminated. Two and a half years later his therapy was recommenced and, from eleven until thirteen (his age at the time of writing) he has attended once weekly.

For me the learning value of this work has been greatly assisted by Dr. Donald Meltzer with whom I have had many opportunities to discuss this material, together with a group of colleagues, in a study group on autism.

My earlier work with Piffie preceded the publication of Frances Tustin's contributions to the understanding of autism. But much of Piffie's material will have a familiar ring to those who have followed her illuminating and sensitive studies on this subject and may be understood as contributing further evidence in support of her findings.

It should be stressed however that the periods of psychotherapy to be discussed mainly concern the residual effects of an autistic state. Piffie was probably beginning to emerge from this state before he commenced psychotherapy and he shed its more blatant manifestations within the first year of therapy. Nevertheless traces of former autistic features may still be discerned and they continue to have a constricting effect upon his development.

Early History and Background

Christopher is the youngest of three children. At the time of his birth, by Caesarian section, his mother was very anxious, having from her previous experiences reason to fear that he might die. In fact he was healthy, but a very passive baby, sleeping a great deal and never grasping the nipple or bottle teat sufficiently strongly to suck properly. Milk had to be practically poured into him.

At about two and a half a medical friend drew his parents’ attention to his condition. At that time his meaningful contact and response to people and things around him was so meagre that the possibilities of his being deaf or mentally defective were investigated.
